titulo: A1 mock test: The most common A1 mistakes and writing

aula.objetivo: Review the whole A1 map, practise reading and listening in the A1 format, avoid the most frequent A1 mistakes that English speakers make, and take a closed mock test. No new grammar.

sessao.titulo: The most common A1 mistakes and writing

blocos.titulo: Six mistakes that English speakers make at A1
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: age uses «avere»: «Ho venti anni», not «Sono venti anni». STEP 2: hunger, thirst, cold and sleepiness also use «avere»: «Ho freddo», not «Sono freddo». STEP 3: to say how you are doing, use «stare»: «Sto bene, grazie». STEP 4: «non» goes before the verb: «Non parlo tedesco». STEP 5: to say that you like something, English makes the person the subject («I like»). In Italian the thing liked is the subject of «piace», and the person appears as «mi»: «Mi piace leggere». STEP 6: with most means of transport, use «in»: «Vado al lavoro in autobus», not «per autobus». STEP 7: before you write a sentence, ask yourself these six questions: the verb for age, the verb for feeling, the verb for how you are, the position of «non», the verb of liking and the preposition for transport.
blocos.comparacao: All six mistakes are copies of English structures: «I am twenty», «I am cold», «I am well», «I do not speak», «I like» and «by bus». Each one is a perfectly natural English sentence, which is exactly why it feels right. The cure is to learn the Italian frame, not the individual word. The corrections are short, so say them aloud until they feel natural.

exemplos.pt: I go to work by bus

erros.motivo: «Sono freddo» describes a cold person. Feeling cold uses «avere».
«Mi» is the person; the thing liked is the subject of «piace».
English «by» does not become «per» here: use «in» with most means of transport.

blocos.titulo: Writing short A1 texts: capitals and punctuation
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: days of the week and months are written in lowercase: «lunedì», «maggio». English capitalizes them. STEP 2: nationalities and languages are also lowercase: «italiano», «brasiliana». STEP 3: names of people, cities and countries keep the capital: «Marco», «Roma», «l'Italia». STEP 4: a question starts with a capital and ends with a question mark, with no special mark at the start. STEP 5: to write a short message, use a greeting, two or three simple sentences and a closing: «Ciao, a presto!». STEP 6: the accent on the final vowel is part of the spelling: «città», «perché», «lunedì». Do not leave it out.
blocos.comparacao: English capitals are generous: days, months, nationalities and languages all start with a capital letter. Italian keeps capitals for names. If you copy the English habit, your text will look wrong even if every word is correct.

erros.motivo: Days of the week are written in lowercase.

itens.enunciado: How do you say «I like reading»?

blocos.enunciado: Write four short sentences about yourself and check each of the six traps one by one: age, feeling, how you are, «non», «mi piace» and transport.
Say the six corrections aloud, one after the other.
